Recent findings suggest that AI is becoming a part of almost everything we do in technology today. Whether it's detecting fraudulent transactions, assessing credit risk, forecasting demand, or personalizing customer experiences, organizations are increasingly relying on AI to make faster and smarter decisions.

Industry observers note that and naturally, when we talk about building AI systems, most of the conversation revolves around model accuracy, performance, and deployment. We spend considerable time making sure our models are trained well, our pipelines run efficiently, and our systems can handle production workloads.

But here's something we don't always pay enough attention to: Can we actually trust the data feeding these models?

After all, even the most sophisticated AI model can produce misleading results if the underlying data is incomplete, inconsistent, or incorrectly interpreted. What's interesting is that these problems don't always show up as technical failures. Sometimes, everything appears to be working perfectly fine.

Imagine a financial institution that has recently deployed an AI-powered loan risk assessment system. The team has spent months preparing the data, training the model, testing its performance, and finally moving it into production.

Recent findings suggest that the deployment goes smoothly. Data pipelines are running on schedule, predictions are being generated, and all the monitoring dashboards are green.

In a recent development, A few weeks later, however, the business team notices something unusual. The model has started classifying more customers as high risk than expected.

The data science team checks the model configuration. Nothing has changed. The engineering team reviews the pipelines. All jobs have completed successfully. Even the infrastructure looks healthy.

It turns out that an upstream source system changed the definition of a customer income field from annual gross income to annual net income. The field name remained the same, the data type was still numeric, and none of the existing technical validations detected the change.

The pipeline continued running as expected, but the model was now receiving information with a different business meaning.

This brings us to an vital point: Just because an AI pipeline runs successfully doesn't necessarily mean we can trust its output.

Building reliable AI systems requires us to look beyond the model itself. We need to understand where the data originates, how it changes as it moves through different systems, whether it meets quality expectations, and who is responsible when something goes wrong.

In this article, we'll explore three important elements of trustworthy AI pipelines (data quality, data lineage, and accountability) and look at how engineering teams can incorporate them into their existing workflows without making the process unnecessarily complicated.

It has been revealed that most modern data pipelines come with some form of operational monitoring. Engineering teams track job completion, execution time, system availability, and processing failures.

These metrics are key because they help us understand whether our systems are functioning as expected.

Operational monitoring primarily tells us whether a pipeline executed successfully. It doesn't necessarily tell us whether the data being processed is accurate, consistent, or suitable for the model consuming it.

Suppose we're building a loan risk model that uses a customer's debt-to-income ratio as one of its input features.

The calculation is straightforward:.

Debt-to-income ratio = Monthly debt payments / Monthly income.

Now imagine that an upstream system starts supplying annual income instead of monthly income.

The calculation still executes successfully. The values are numeric, the transformation doesn't throw an error, and the model continues generating predictions.

However, the resulting debt-to-income ratio is incorrect because the numerator and denominator represent different time periods.

This is where traditional monitoring falls short.

To build trustworthy AI pipelines, we need to look at different dimensions of system health.

These approaches complement each other.

In a recent development, A pipeline can be operationally healthy while processing unreliable data. Similarly, a model can continue producing predictions even when the meaning of an notable input field has changed.

For engineering teams, the objective should be to identify these problems as early as possible, ideally before they reach downstream models.

We've all heard the phrase "garbage in, garbage out.".

And despite all the progress we've made in artificial intelligence, this principle hasn't changed.

AI models may be capable of processing enormous volumes of data and identifying complex patterns, but they cannot automatically guarantee that the information they're receiving is correct.

This is where data quality becomes important.

Data quality refers to how well information meets the requirements of its intended use. In AI pipelines, it helps us determine whether incoming data is sufficiently reliable for model training, evaluation, or inference.

Let's look at four dimensions that are particularly relevant.

Imagine we're developing a loan risk model that relies on customer income, outstanding debt, repayment history, and credit utilization.

What happens if 20% of the incoming records are missing income information?

Industry observers note that should we reject those records? Should we replace missing values using an approved statistical method? Or should we flag them for additional review?

There isn't one answer that works for every system.

The right approach depends on the model, the business requirements, and the potential consequences of the decision.

What matters is that missing information is handled deliberately.

For example, replacing missing income with zero may allow the pipeline to continue running, but it could significantly distort the model's predictions.

Validity checks whether values meet expected formats, ranges, and business rules.

Consider a customer record containing the following information:.

The credit utilization value immediately stands out.

Although credit utilization can exceed 100% in certain circumstances, a value of 450% may warrant investigation.

This highlights an crucial distinction: Not every unusual value is incorrect, and not every technically valid value is meaningful.

A database may accept any numeric value, but the business may need additional rules to determine whether that value is appropriate for the model.

Engineering teams should distinguish between invalid records, unexpected observations, and legitimate exceptions.

This is one of the most common challenges in enterprise data environments.

Imagine two systems providing customer income information.

System A reports annual gross income.

System B reports monthly net income.

Both datasets contain a column called income.

If we combine these datasets without understanding their definitions, we risk introducing inconsistencies into downstream calculations.

The data may look perfectly fine from a technical perspective. The problem is that the same field represents different business concepts.

This is why data definitions, units, and transformation rules are just as important as schema validation.

Suppose a model predicts a customer's current financial risk using income information that was last updated 18 months ago.

The data might be accurate, complete, and consistent.

But is it current enough to support the decision?

Different AI applications have different freshness requirements.

A real-time fraud detection model may require near-real-time transaction information, while a long-term forecasting model may work with less frequently updated datasets.

The important thing is to define these expectations based on how the data will be used.

The good news is that improving data quality doesn't always require sophisticated enterprise tools.

A practical starting point is to define validation rules for the most key input fields.

For example, consider the following conceptual configuration:.

This is an illustrative data quality contract rather than executable configuration for a particular framework.

It defines basic expectations and specifies what should happen when the data fails validation.

Tools such as Great Expectations can help automate these checks. For smaller systems, custom SQL or Python validations may be sufficient.

However, technical validation alone isn't enough.

Remember our original example where the income field changed from gross to net income?

Both values could easily pass a rule requiring income to be greater than zero.

Detecting that kind of issue requires clear business definitions, communication with upstream systems, and appropriate change management.

In other words, data quality isn't just about checking values. It's also about understanding what those values represent.

Now let's assume our loan risk model generates an unexpectedly high risk score for a customer.

The model output is available, but we want to understand what contributed to the prediction.

We start investigating the input data.

The income information came from a customer application system. Outstanding debt came from another database. Both datasets went through several transformations before reaching the feature engineering pipeline.

The final features were then passed to the model.

At this point, a seemingly simple question becomes surprisingly difficult:.

Where exactly did the information used for this prediction come from?

This is where data lineage becomes valuable.

Data lineage describes how data originates, moves, and changes across different systems.

For AI pipelines, it helps us understand the journey from raw source data to the features used by a model.

A simplified flow might look like this:.

Source Systems → Data Transformation → Feature Engineering → Model Inference → Predictions.

Each stage introduces dependencies that can affect downstream results.

Data lineage can be captured at different levels of detail.

Dataset-level lineage demonstrates relationships between datasets.

Loan Applications → Cleaned Applications → Model Features.

This helps us understand how datasets move through the overall architecture.

However, suppose the model's debt-to-income ratio suddenly changes.

Dataset-level lineage might tell us which datasets were involved, but it may not provide enough detail to identify the affected field.

That's where column-level lineage becomes useful.

debt_to_income_ratio = monthly_debt_payment / monthly_income.

Column-level lineage can show that the resulting feature depends on two upstream attributes.

If one of those attributes changes, engineers can trace the dependency and investigate the impact.

This is especially valuable in environments where multiple reports, applications, and AI models depend on shared data sources.

Large organizations may use dedicated metadata management and lineage platforms.

However, smaller teams can start by capturing essential metadata during pipeline execution.

OpenLineage provides an open standard for collecting and exchanging lineage metadata across supported systems.

For more detailed prediction-level investigations, teams may also need to retain feature snapshots or inference logs, subject to privacy and retention requirements.

It's important to understand that lineage doesn't automatically guarantee data accuracy.

A pipeline can be perfectly documented and still contain incorrect transformation logic.

But when something goes wrong, lineage gives engineering teams a clearer starting point for investigation.

Instead of searching across multiple systems and trying to reconstruct dependencies manually, they can identify where data originated and how it changed along the way.

Let's consider another situation.

An AI model starts producing unexpected results.

The data science team checks the model and finds no complications.

The data engineering team confirms that the pipelines are running successfully.

The source-system team verifies that data was delivered according to its interface.

Yet the problem remains unresolved.

Everyone has completed their individual checks, but nobody has identified who should coordinate the investigation.

This is where accountability becomes important.

Industry observers note that AI pipelines often involve multiple teams responsible for different stages of the data lifecycle. Without clearly defined ownership, even relatively simple challenges can take longer to resolve.

A practical accountability framework should distinguish between three responsibilities.

Data owners are responsible for defining the business meaning and expected quality of critical information.

For example, someone needs to determine whether an income field represents gross income, net income, or another financial measure.

These definitions should be documented and communicated to downstream consumers.

Data engineering and platform teams typically manage data ingestion, transformations, validation mechanisms, and pipeline operations.

Their responsibilities may include implementing quality checks, monitoring failures, and assessing the technical impact of changes.

However, technical teams shouldn't be expected to make business-definition decisions without appropriate input.

Data science and ML engineering teams are responsible for evaluating model behavior, managing model versions, and assessing how changes in input data may affect predictions.

If a critical feature changes, the model team may need to determine whether additional testing, recalibration, or retraining is required.

Defining ownership is useful, but connecting it to an operational process is even more key.

Consider a critical data quality failure during feature generation.

A response process might look like this:.

The exact workflow will vary depending on the organization and the risk associated with the application.

The objective is to ensure that technical alerts lead to clear actions.

After all, an alert that nobody owns is just another notification waiting to be ignored.

So far, we've discussed why data quality, lineage, and accountability matter.

But how can we bring these concepts into everyday engineering practices?

Here are five controls that teams can introduce without redesigning their entire architecture.

Data contracts define expectations between data producers and consumers.

They can document schemas, field definitions, units, freshness requirements, and compatibility expectations.

For example, rather than specifying only that annual_income is numeric, a contract should clarify whether it represents gross or net income, the currency, and the applicable time period.

This reduces the risk of downstream systems misinterpreting technically valid information.

Quality gates validate critical data before it progresses through the pipeline.

These checks can be implemented during ingestion, transformation, feature generation, or inference.

For example, a feature engineering process calculating debt-to-income ratios should verify that debt and income values use compatible time periods.

Failure handling should reflect the severity of the glitch. Some records may be quarantined, while more serious failures may require stopping the pipeline.

Pipeline execution should produce sufficient metadata to identify source datasets, transformations, and downstream outputs.

Where appropriate, teams should also capture model and feature versions associated with predictions.

This information supports impact analysis, debugging, and investigation when unexpected results occur.

AI systems evolve continuously.

Datasets change, transformation logic is updated, features are modified, and models are retrained.

Versioning helps engineering teams understand which components were active at a particular point in time.

Relevant evidence may include pipeline configurations, dataset snapshots, model versions, validation outcomes, and deployment records.

Retention should be designed around operational requirements, privacy considerations, and applicable policies rather than storing everything indefinitely.

Every critical data element or pipeline component should have an identified owner or responsible team.

More importantly, ownership should connect directly to incident management and change approval processes.

If a source definition changes, teams should know who evaluates the impact.

If a quality gate fails, the responsible team should receive the alert.

If model performance deteriorates, the investigation should have a clear escalation path.

These controls are most effective when they become part of normal development and deployment practices rather than separate administrative activities.

Implementing comprehensive governance across an entire data environment can be challenging, particularly for organizations with legacy systems and complex dependencies.

A more effective approach is to begin with one critical AI pipeline.

For example, a team operating a loan risk model could start by identifying the inputs that have the greatest influence on its predictions.

These might include income, outstanding debt, repayment history, and credit utilization.

For each critical input, the team can document five things:.

Once these foundations are established, the team can implement automated checks and gradually extend the approach to additional datasets.

This incremental strategy also makes it easier to demonstrate the value of governance controls.

For instance, teams can track how swiftly data-related incidents are detected, how long investigations take, and whether recurring problems are reduced.

The goal isn't to introduce governance for its own sake.

It's to improve the reliability, maintainability, and transparency of the systems developers are responsible for operating.

Explainable AI has become an important topic in machine learning.

Techniques such as feature importance analysis and SHAP can help teams understand which inputs influence model predictions.

However, explainability and data trustworthiness address different problems.

Suppose a model explanation identifies debt-to-income ratio as a major contributor to a customer's high-risk classification.

That explanation may accurately describe the model's behavior.

But if the debt-to-income ratio was calculated using an incorrectly defined income field, the explanation alone may not reveal the underlying data problem.

This highlights the importance of evaluating AI systems across multiple dimensions.

Model explainability helps us understand how predictions are generated.

Data quality helps establish whether inputs satisfy defined expectations.

Data lineage provides visibility into where information originated and how it was transformed.

Accountability ensures that identified problems can be investigated and addressed.

These capabilities are complementary rather than interchangeable.

In a recent development, none independently guarantees that an AI system is accurate, fair, secure, or compliant. Together, however, they provide a stronger foundation for evaluating and improving system reliability.

As AI systems become more integrated into business processes, engineering teams face increasing expectations around reliability, transparency, and accountability.

Model accuracy and operational performance remain essential, but they represent only part of the overall picture.

A pipeline can execute successfully while processing inconsistent information. A model can generate predictions using features whose definitions have changed. And an explanation can describe a model's behavior without identifying problems in the underlying data.

Building trustworthy AI therefore requires attention to the entire data lifecycle.

Data quality controls help detect unreliable inputs. Lineage provides visibility into how information moves through systems. Clear ownership ensures that concerns can be investigated and resolved.

Importantly, these practices don't need to begin with large-scale governance programs or expensive technology investments.

Engineering teams can start with a single critical pipeline, identify its most important data elements, establish quality expectations, and introduce basic traceability and accountability mechanisms.

Over time, these practices can become part of standard development and deployment workflows.

Sources indicate that the real measure of a trustworthy AI pipeline isn't simply whether it produces a prediction. It's whether the organization can understand, validate, and take responsibility for the information behind that prediction.

After all, a green dashboard is reassuring. But it shouldn't be the only evidence that an AI system is working as intended.

It asks the court to declare state gambling laws preempted. It also seeks to stop Louisiana from enforcing or extending the state order.

Industry observers note that maine's Gambling Control Unit is heading toward an early 2027 launch of tribal-run online casinos after a single public hearing. A former lawmaker warns that the state's behavioral health system is too thin for a possible rise in gambling addiction, while a federal lawsuit still targets the tribes' exclusivity.

Maine’s regulator is moving toward an early 2027 launch of tribal-run online casinos. Only one public hearing has been held so far. WGME’s I-Team reported on Nov. 16 that the Gambling Control Unit began iGaming rulemaking in June. Residents in the report raised a separate concern. They worry the state lacks the mental health and problem-gambling resources to cope.

According to recent reports, maine will become the eighth state with legal online casinos. Its four Wabanaki tribes hold exclusive licenses under LD 1164, the Wabanaki internet gaming act. The Legislature lists the measure as enacted as Public Law 538.

In a recent development, the money set aside for addiction services is small next to the state’s cut. The legislative fiscal note sends 2% of adjusted gross iGaming receipts to the Gambling Addiction Prevention and Treatment Fund. The state’s own 18% share is projected at $1.8 million in fiscal 2025-26 and $3.6 million in fiscal 2026-27.

Critics doubt the system can absorb the demand. Patty Locuratolo Hymanson, a neurologist and former state lawmaker, told WGME that Maine lacks the behavioral health resources to handle a possible rise in gambling addiction from online casinos.

Lawmakers reshaped the revenue split before passage. A committee amendment raised the state’s share from 16% to 18%. The same amendment cut the opioid treatment fund’s allocation from 3% to 1.5%. The fiscal note also carries ongoing General Fund appropriations of $645,354 for six Gambling Control Unit positions. Those include two criminal intelligence analysts and two auditors.

Sources indicate that the regulator itself was skeptical at first. Before the bill became law, Executive Director Milt Champion opposed it in written testimony. He argued iGaming wasn’t warranted while sports wagering was only in its second year.

Sources indicate that rulemaking is still underway. The unit issued its third version of the draft rules on Sept. 30, 2026, and took comments until Oct. 30. Champion has warned that major revisions would force a fourth publication. The third draft keeps the tax rate on adjusted gross receipts unchanged. It also retains the license fee and bond requirements. The regulator is hiring six staff members dedicated to iGaming.

According to recent reports, the launch also faces a court fight over tribal exclusivity. Churchill Downs and Oxford Casino Hotel brought their suit against the Gambling Control Unit and Champion in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maine. They are asking the court to declare the law unconstitutional. The challenge goes to the heart of the market’s design, which reserves online casino licenses for the tribes.

The next deadlines are procedural. Under Maine’s rulemaking law, the unit has up to 120 days after comments close to adopt the rules. The Attorney General’s office has up to 150 days from that same date to approve them as legal. The unit’s rulemaking page also lists a public hearing notice marked Nov. 30, 2026, which could change that timetable.

According to recent reports, A 3D model can look convincing in a still image and still be awkward on a website. The real questions appear when someone rotates it, loads it on a typical connection, or views it on a narrow phone screen. AI generators have made the first draft of a model cheap, which shifts the work toward the part developers and designers already know: budgets, testing and fallbacks.

This article walks through a web-readiness review for an AI-generated model, using an openwork ceramic vessel generated from a single reference image with Tripo as the worked example. The checks apply equally to output from other generators. It includes a small Node.js script that audits a GLB file against a size budget, and the markup for a lightweight viewer with a static fallback. The model shown is one candidate, so it cannot prove browser speed, mobile behavior, hidden geometry or export compatibility. Those are checks to run on your own asset.

Recent findings suggest that traditional 3D work involves modeling, polygon layout, materials, scale and export. AI generation can shorten the blank-workspace stage. A beginner may discover the category through a search such as AI 3D model generator free, but an initial candidate is useful only if it survives review.

Recent findings suggest that for this vessel, start with the negative space, meaning the openings between the ribs. A flattering front view can hide a blocked cavity, a thin wall, or two surfaces passing through each other. Generation moves the bottleneck from making a first shape to deciding whether that shape is usable.

Image-to-3D tools use a visual reference to create a model candidate, while text-to-3D routes start from a written prompt. Tripo offers both, and other hosted options include Meshy, Rodin by Hyper3D and 3D AI Studio, all of which list GLB among their export formats, while open-source models such as TripoSR and Stable Fast 3D let you run generation yourself. Features, pricing, licensing and output quality differ and change often, so check each vendor’s current documentation. The image route suits this example because the folds, uneven rim and openings already exist in the source.

Recent findings suggest that whichever tool you use, it can provide a candidate for inspection. It cannot decide whether the source is licensed, whether the unseen rear structure is believable, or whether the exported asset suits a particular viewer. Those judgments belong to the person publishing the page.

Sources indicate that give the object one job. In a portfolio, this vessel might show how its shell and openings relate. That is narrower than calling it printable, manufacturable or dimensionally accurate. Note what must remain recognizable, and provide a still image if the interactive view fails.

Use an image you own or have permission to reuse. Busy backgrounds can distract an image-based workflow, so isolate the object when possible. One photograph also leaves the back and underside unknown. Treat those areas as review risks, not as details confirmed by the source.

After generation, rotate beyond the familiar front. Check the rear, top, underside and sides. Trace each large opening. Look for merged ribs, intersecting surfaces or an unstable base. A wireframe view, when available, can expose crowded geometry. A single front-facing candidate cannot answer these hidden-angle questions, so check them on your own model.

Sources indicate that record the download size, polygon count and texture dimensions. Polygons are the small flat faces that form the shape, and web viewers draw them as triangles. This matters because generator defaults are often tuned for quality, not for the web. In the generation screenshot for this vessel, the viewer reports roughly 1.95 million faces and the settings show 4K texture quality. That is a fine starting point for inspection but a heavy asset for a phone on a mobile connection. Curved ribs may need many triangles, but the count should still fit your page budget.

In a recent development, glTF is the open format most web viewers expect, and GLB is its single-file form that can bundle geometry, textures and materials. The format does not guarantee good performance, so measure the package. The script below reads a GLB with the open-source glTF Transform library, counts triangles, lists texture sizes, and compares them with a budget. The budget values are placeholders; set your own from your target devices.

According to recent reports, run it with node audit.mjs model.glb after installing @gltf-transform/core. It exits with a non-zero status when the asset is over budget, so you can run it in CI. A short test builds two GLBs with known triangle counts, one small and one with 200,000 triangles, and checks that the first passes and the second fails with the right message:.

In a recent development, when an asset fails, glTF Transform also has a command line. gltf-transform inspect model.glb reports what is inside a file, and gltf-transform optimize input.glb output.glb --compress draco --texture-compress webp applies geometry and texture compression. Compression and mesh simplification can introduce artifacts, especially around thin ribs and openings, so reopen the result and re-check the angles from Gate 3 instead of accepting a smaller file blindly. Also check that your viewer supports the compression you choose.

Load the asset in the intended viewer at desktop and phone widths. Check framing, touch rotation, keyboard access, scrolling and a slower connection. The Google-backed model-viewer web component is one low-code option, and libraries such as three.js give you more control at the cost of more code. The markup below shows the pieces that matter for a first release: a poster image that loads first, lazy loading so the heavy file waits until needed, a text alternative, and visible controls.

In a recent development, the alt text, a poster and touch-action="pan-y" (so a vertical swipe still scrolls the page on a phone) address the common failures. Check the current model-viewer documentation for attribute names and the recommended script include, since they can change between versions. Also consider the WCAG guidance on non-text content: provide a useful description, and offer instructions plus a static image for people who cannot operate the viewer.

A single front-facing candidate is enough to discuss the method, not to certify a finished web asset. Call it a prototype until the exported file passes the checks required by its actual destination.

In a recent development, the same review pattern can be adapted to an architectural ornament, exhibition object, packaging concept or game prop, but each destination adds its own geometry, scale and delivery requirements. A portfolio may accept an inferred rear surface if that limitation is clear. A sales page, printable file or measured product needs stronger references and technical validation.

In a recent development, the audit script counts triangles, texture sizes and file size only. It does not detect self-intersections, thin walls, flipped normals or licensing problems, and passing it does not make an asset good. The budget numbers are illustrative, and real limits depend on your audience’s devices and connections. Tool features and terms change, so verify them with the vendor before you rely on them, and treat any speed or quality claims on vendor pages as the vendor’s own.

It has been revealed that inspect the angle you would normally crop out. Confirm input rights, measure the download, and test touch, keyboard and a slow connection. Reread the surrounding copy, because claims of fabrication accuracy or production readiness need supporting evidence. For this vessel, “exploratory web model” is an honest label, and more demanding claims require better references and a specialist review.

Decide what visitors should learn or do before adding a 3D viewer. A modest prototype with a useful fallback can beat a dramatic asset that loads slowly or hides limitations.

Industry observers note that do I need to code to create a model with an AI generator? No code is required to generate an initial model candidate in Tripo or similar tools. Publishing it interactively is separate work and usually involves a viewer, hosting, responsive testing and enough HTML or JavaScript knowledge to diagnose problems.

It has been revealed that when should I use image-to-3D instead of text-to-3D? Use image-to-3D when a rights-cleared visual should guide the form, and text-to-3D when the idea begins as words. Do not treat the two routes as interchangeable evidence.

Is a generated model ready to publish as soon as it exports? No. Inspect the shape from several angles, measure the delivery package, test the intended viewer and prepare a fallback. Higher-stakes uses may also need specialist geometry, scale, material and rights review.

Sources indicate that how can a beginner keep web 3D manageable? Give one object one clear job. Set a file-size target, test desktop and phone widths, keep interaction simple, and retain a still image for readers who cannot load or operate the viewer.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that google designed TPUs from the ground up to be exceptionally efficient for machine learning workloads, delivering top-tier performance per total cost of ownership (TCO). Because TPUs trade general-purpose hardware scheduling for wide systolic arrays, dedicated SparseCore engines, and custom interconnect fabrics, adhering to specific architectural best practices is essential to achieve maximum performance. To help developers get the most out of TPUs, we are launching the open-source AI-Hypercomputer/tpu-codesign guide. This post highlights its key principles—spanning shape alignment, architectural choices like LatentMoE, and parallelism strategies—to accelerate LLMs, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, and other hardware-intensive workloads on TPUs.

Performance tuning starts with model definition. Architectural choices made before the first training step set permanent ceilings on MFU (Model FLOP Utilization), cost, and serving latency. This guide gives concrete, hardware-grounded design rules for teams building or adapting models for TPUs, organized into three groups:.

In a recent development, how to use this guide. The shape rules apply to anyone designing a new model. If you are adapting an existing model rather than designing one, the Expressing Parallelism section applies without touching the checkpoint. The general rules hold for any large-matmul architecture (dense LLMs, multimodal, and world models), and the companion AI-Hypercomputer/tpu-codesign repository grows model- and workload-specific sections over time.

Eighth-generation TPUs. These principles carry forward to TPU 8t and TPU 8i and to the newly announced TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max. The reasoning stays the same and the thresholds move with the hardware. TPU 8t and TPU 8i both add native FP4. For training, TPU 8t also brings more balanced Vector Processing Unit (VPU) scaling. For serving, TPU 8i adds the Boardfly topology, a Collectives Acceleration Engine (CAE), and 3x more on-chip SRAM. We note the effects inline in Principles 5–8, and follow-up posts will cover eighth-generation designs in depth.

Measured evidence. Alongside the published sources, notes marked Measured carry results from our own Ironwood profiling program: open 20–30B MoEs (a Qwen3-30B-derived LatentMoE variant; GPT-OSS-20B) plus dense controls, single slice (except for the 512-chip TPU v7x and 1,024-chip TPU v4 ablations in Principle 4), BF16, training shapes up to 32K sequence, all against tuned-systems baselines. Treat the trends and rankings as transferable, the exact percentages as config-specific.

TPUs are purpose-built custom ML ASICs designed from the ground up to deliver state-of-the-art performance per total cost of ownership (TCO). While their architectural choices—such as wide 256×256 systolic arrays, software-managed VMEM, dedicated SparseCore engines, and direct multi-dimensional ICI fabrics—enable exceptional efficiency, they inherently create specific structural constraints and programming patterns that must be carefully followed to unlock maximal performance. Reaching peak efficiency requires aligning model shapes, routing, and parallelism directly with these underlying hardware characteristics:.

Michigan online casino revenue rises 16.7% in October as US iGaming growth slows

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (518 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Readwrite

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Michigan's online casinos generated $305.3 million in adjusted gross receipts in October, up 16.7% from a year earlier.
  • Michigan’s online casino market kept growing at a double-digit rate in October.
  • The October result followed a soft patch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Michigan's online casinos generated $305.3 million in adjusted gross receipts in October, up 16.7% from a year earlier. The double-digit gain comes as national iGaming growth cools, though Michigan's own pace has slowed from a year ago.

Michigan’s online casino market kept growing at a double-digit rate in October. Gross receipts came to $318.1 million, according to figures the Michigan Gaming Control Board released Nov. 18. It was the state’s second-best iGaming month of 2026. Only March, with a record $309.1 million in AGR, was higher. March also holds the monthly gross receipts record of $322.1 million, which topped the $315.8 million from December 2025.

The October result followed a soft patch. September AGR was $288.15 million, 0.9% lower than in August.

According to recent reports, the year-over-year gain stands out against the national backdrop. Citizens JMP Securities estimated that US iGaming revenue grew 12% in the third quarter of 2026, the slowest pace it has recorded. Growth had been 19% in the first quarter and 16% in the second. The same data put Michigan’s third-quarter iGaming growth at 17%. Only Delaware, at 36%, and West Virginia, at 26%, grew faster.

According to recent reports, michigan’s own pace has still slowed sharply. In October 2025, online casino AGR grew 31.8% year over year, nearly double this October’s rate. That month produced $261.7 million in AGR and $278.5 million in gross receipts, a record at the time.

It has been revealed that the Michigan figures also invite comparison with Pennsylvania. Its online casinos generated $278,845,570 in October revenue, a state record for Pennsylvania. That figure came in a release issued Nov. 17, a day before Michigan published its October numbers.

It has been revealed that the year-over-year numbers show where Michigan’s growth comes from. Online sports betting AGR fell 3.3% from October 2025. For all of 2025, sportsbooks produced $435.9 million in AGR, while iGaming generated $3.1 billion in gross receipts. Online casino play therefore accounts for most of the state’s online gambling revenue.

Sources indicate that october sportsbook figures swung sharply from one month to the next. Sports betting AGR jumped 91.3% from September. Handle rose 11.1% to $605.4 million, and sportsbook gross receipts reached $70.7 million. Combined online casino and sports betting gross receipts totaled $388.8 million.

Industry observers note that the broader online market had been growing faster earlier in the year. From January through July, combined online casino and sports betting AGR totaled $2.21 billion, up 20.9% from the same period in 2025. October’s casino growth is consistent with a market that is still expanding, but at a slower rate than a year ago.

Tribal online operators also made $8.9 million in payments to their governing bodies for October.

What Is BIO Tagging and How to Use It for Document AI Training Data

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2687 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish

Industry observers note that if you've worked with named entity recognition (NER) in text, you've probably seen BIO tagging before. It's the standard way to mark where entities start, continue, and end inside a sequence of tokens. What you might not know is that the same tagging scheme has become the backbone of document AI -- the field where machine learning models extract structured data from invoices, receipts, contracts, and other business documents.

In a recent development, this guide explains how BIO tagging works, why it matters for document understanding, and how to build BIO-tagged training data that actually produces accurate models. We'll walk through the tagging logic, show real examples on financial documents, cover common mistakes that silently hurt model performance, and look at tools that speed up the annotation process.

BIO stands for Beginning, Inside, Outside. It's a labeling scheme that tells a model which tokens belong to an entity, which tokens continue that entity, and which tokens are just background noise.

● B (Beginning) -- the first token of a named entity.

● I (Inside) -- any token that continues the same entity.

● O (Outside) -- any token that doesn't belong to any entity.

According to recent reports, take a simple line from an invoice: "Invoice #INV-2024-0891". If you're labeling invoice numbers, the BIO tags look like this:.

Token          Label ─────          ───── Invoice        O #              O INV-2024-0891  B-invoice_number.

Now consider a multi-word entity like a vendor name: "Acme Corporation Ltd". All three words are part of the same entity, so the tagging becomes:.

Token          Label ─────          ───── Acme           B-vendor_name Corporation    I-vendor_name Ltd            I-vendor_name.

The B prefix marks where the entity starts. The I prefix marks every following token that belongs to the same entity. Everything else gets O. This three-label structure is simple, but it gives models enough information to learn entity boundaries precisely -- even when two entities of the same type appear next to each other.

Traditional NER works on plain text -- a flat sequence of words. Document AI is harder because pages have two dimensions. A word's meaning depends not just on what comes before and after it in reading order, but also on where it sits on the page. The number "$4,250.00" could be an invoice total, a line item price, or a tax amount depending on its position relative to headers and columns.

It has been revealed that models like LayoutLMv3, LiLT, and BROS solve this by combining text tokens with their bounding box coordinates. Each token gets three inputs: the word itself, its position on the page (x, y, width, height), and its BIO label during training. The model learns to associate spatial patterns with entity types.

According to recent reports, BIO tagging fits this architecture perfectly because it operates at the token level. Every word on the page gets exactly one label, and the model learns from thousands of these labeled tokens which spatial and textual patterns correspond to which fields.

If you're coming from a background in natural language processing in Python, the concept is identical -- BIO tagging works the same way whether your tokens come from a sentence or a document page. The difference is that document AI adds positional data to each token.

According to recent reports, BIO isn't the only tagging scheme. You'll encounter several variants:.

● BIO (IOB2) -- B marks the first token, I marks continuation tokens, O marks non-entities. The most widely used scheme.

In a recent development, ● BIOES -- adds E (End) for the last token of a multi-word entity and S (Single) for single-token entities. More explicit boundary marking.

● BILOU -- adds L (Last) and U (Unit). Functionally identical to BIOES with different letters.

It has been revealed that ● IOB1 -- the original scheme where B is only used when two entities of the same type are adjacent. Rarely used today.

In a recent development, for document AI, standard BIO (IOB2) is the safest choice. Here's why:.

● LayoutLMv3 and most pre-trained document models expect BIO format out of the box.

● The FUNSD and CORD benchmark datasets use BIO, so your data format matches the academic baselines.

● BIOES adds more label types, which means you need more training data to learn each one reliably.

● Converting from BIO to BIOES is trivial if you later need it, but the reverse can lose information.

Unless your model architecture specifically requires BIOES or BILOU, stick with BIO.

Recent findings suggest that before you tag a single token, you need a clear label taxonomy -- the list of entity types your model will learn to recognize. A poorly designed taxonomy creates confusion during annotation and cascades into model errors.

Ask yourself: what fields does the downstream system need? For invoice processing, a typical taxonomy looks like this:.

vendor_name vendor_address invoice_number invoice_date due_date line_item_description line_item_quantity line_item_price subtotal tax total payment_method currency.

**Rule 1 -- One label per semantic meaning. **Don't reuse amount for both line item prices and the invoice total. A model that learns "amount" means two different things depending on context will confuse them on novel layouts.

In a recent development, **Rule 2 -- Use hierarchical names. **Once your taxonomy exceeds 10 labels, flat names start colliding. line_item_price is better than price because it's self-documenting and prevents collisions with total_price.

**Rule 3 -- Include a catch-all label. **Call it other or O. Text that doesn't belong to any entity still needs a label for token classification. Without negative examples, the model can't learn what isn't a field.

**Rule 4 -- Match your model architecture. **Token classification models like LayoutLMv3 work best with fine-grained, word-level labels. Generative models like Donut output structured text, so they work with coarser labels. Choose your model first, then design labels to match.

Here's the practical workflow for turning raw PDF documents into BIO-tagged training data ready for model training.

Your model needs both the text and its coordinates on the page. For digitally generated PDFs, extract the text layer directly:.

import pdfplumber def extract_words(pdf_path):     words = []     with pdfplumber.open(pdf_path) as pdf:         for page in pdf.pages:             for word in page.extract_words():                 words.append({                     'text': word['text'],                     'bbox': [word['x0'], word['top'],                              word['x1'], word['bottom']],                     'page': page.page_number                 })     return words.

For scanned documents, you'll need OCR. Tesseract is the standard open-source option:.

import pytesseract from pdf2image import convert_from_path def ocr_pdf(pdf_path, dpi=300):     images = convert_from_path(pdf_path, dpi=dpi)     all_words = []     for i, img in enumerate(images):         data = pytesseract.image_to_data(             img, output_type=pytesseract.Output.DICT         )         for j in range(len(data['text'])):             if data['text'][j].strip():                 all_words.append({                     'text': data['text'][j],                     'bbox': [data['left'][j], data['top'][j],                              data['left'][j] + data['width'][j],                              data['top'][j] + data['height'][j]],                     'page': i + 1                 })     return all_words.

In a recent development, models expect coordinates normalized to a 0--1000 range. This makes the model resolution-independent -- a word at the top-left corner is at (0, 0) whether the page is 72 DPI or 300 DPI.

def normalize_bbox(bbox, page_width, page_height):     return [         int(1000 bbox[0] / page_width), *        int(1000 *bbox[1] / page_height),         int(1000 bbox[2] / page_width), *        int(1000 *bbox[3] / page_height)     ].

If you've worked with bounding box annotation for document AI, you'll recognize this normalization step -- it's the same coordinate transformation used across all document understanding models.

This is the annotation step. For each word in the document, assign the appropriate BIO label based on what field it represents. Here's what a fully labeled invoice line looks like:.

words = [     {'text': 'Invoice',      'label': 'O'},     {'text': 'Date:',        'label': 'O'},     {'text': 'March',        'label': 'B-invoice_date'},     {'text': '15,',          'label': 'I-invoice_date'},     {'text': '2024',         'label': 'I-invoice_date'},     {'text': 'Total:',       'label': 'O'},     {'text': '$4,250.00',    'label': 'B-total'},     {'text': 'Acme',         'label': 'B-vendor_name'},     {'text': 'Corporation',  'label': 'I-vendor_name'}, ].

According to recent reports, notice that "March 15, 2024" is a single entity spanning three tokens. The first token gets B-invoice_date, and the following tokens get I-invoice_date. The model learns that these tokens form one continuous entity.

According to recent reports, layoutLMv3 expects training data in a specific JSON structure. Each document becomes one training example with parallel arrays for words, bounding boxes, and labels:.

{   "id": "invoice_001",   "words": ["Invoice", "Date:", "March", "15,", "2024",              "Total:", "$4,250.00", "Acme", "Corporation"],   "bboxes": [[84, 42, 145, 58], [84, 62, 120, 78],              [130, 62, 172, 78], [175, 62, 195, 78],              [198, 62, 230, 78], [84, 320, 125, 336],              [130, 320, 210, 336], [84, 22, 125, 38],              [130, 22, 210, 38]],   "labels": ["O", "O", "B-invoice_date", "I-invoice_date",              "I-invoice_date", "O", "B-total",              "B-vendor_name", "I-vendor_name"] }.

If you're working with large volumes of documents, this guide on building JSON training datasets from PDFs covers how to automate much of this conversion pipeline.

Industry observers note that manually labeling every word on every page is slow. A single invoice might have 200-400 tokens, and you need hundreds of labeled documents for a usable model. Here are three approaches to speed things up.

Sources indicate that many financial fields follow predictable patterns. Dates, currency amounts, and invoice numbers can be pre-labeled with regex before a human annotator reviews them:.

import re PATTERNS = {     'invoice_date': [         r'\b\d{1,2}[/-]\d{1,2}[/-]\d{2,4}\b',         r'\b(?:Jan|Feb|Mar|Apr|May|Jun|Jul|Aug|Sep|Oct|Nov|Dec)\w*\s+\d{1,2},?\s+\d{4}\b'     ],     'total': [         r'$[\d,]+.\d{2}\b'     ],     'invoice_number': [         r'\b(?:INV|inv)[- ]?\d{4,}\b'     ] } def pre_label(words):     for word in words:         word['label'] = 'O'  # default         for label, patterns in PATTERNS.items():             for pattern in patterns:                 if re.match(pattern, word['text']):                     word['label'] = f'B-{label}'                     break     return words.

In a recent development, this won't catch everything -- vendor names, addresses, and line item descriptions need human judgment. But it can pre-fill 30-40% of the labels on a typical invoice, turning the annotator's job from labeling to reviewing.

Train a preliminary model on your first 50 labeled documents, then use it to predict labels on new documents. The annotator reviews and corrects the predictions instead of labeling from scratch. As the model improves, corrections become rarer and annotation speed increases.

Industry observers note that the key is selecting documents where the model is least confident for the next round of human review. This focuses annotator time where it has the most impact on model accuracy.

It has been revealed that if you're working with standard financial documents and want to skip the manual pipeline entirely, platforms like AI Asset Management can auto-generate structured labels from raw PDFs -- typically returning results in under 30 seconds per document. The annotator's role shifts from labeling to quality review, which is significantly faster than tagging every token by hand.

It has been revealed that these are the errors that show up most often when teams start building document AI training data. Each one silently degrades model performance.

In a recent development, if "Acme Corporation" is labeled as one entity on page 1 but "Acme" and "Corporation" are labeled as separate entities on page 5, the model receives contradictory training signals. Pick a convention and enforce it across your entire dataset. For vendor names, include the full legal name ("Acme Corporation Ltd") every time.

A common beginner mistake is labeling every token of a multi-word entity with B instead of using B for the first token and I for the rest. "March 15, 2024" should be B-date, I-date, I-date -- not B-date, B-date, B-date. The B-B-B pattern tells the model these are three separate entities, which is wrong.

The word "Total:" is a header, not a value. Only the actual value ($4,250.00) should be tagged as B-total. Labeling "Total:" as part of the entity teaches the model to include headers in its extractions, which corrupts downstream processing.

Some OCR engines split punctuation into separate tokens. "$4,250.00" might become ["$", "4,250", ".", "00"]. If you label only "4,250" and skip the dollar sign and cents, the model learns incomplete extraction patterns. Make sure every token in the entity is covered by B or I tags.

In a recent development, if 95% of your tokens are labeled O and only 0.5% are B-invoice_number, the model will learn that predicting O is almost always correct. This is the class imbalance problem. It's normal for O to dominate, but watch for entity types that appear in fewer than 1% of tokens -- those need more training examples or the model won't learn them reliably.

Before you start training, run these checks on your labeled data. Catching errors here is cheaper than debugging a confused model later.

An I-vendor_name tag should never appear without a preceding B-vendor_name. If it does, either the B tag was missed or the entity boundaries are wrong.

def validate_bio_sequences(labels):     errors = []     for i, label in enumerate(labels):         if label.startswith('I-'):             entity_type = label[2:]             if i == 0:                 errors.append(f'I-{entity_type} at position 0 with no preceding B tag')             else:                 prev = labels[i - 1]                 if prev != f'B-{entity_type}' and prev != f'I-{entity_type}':                     errors.append(f'I-{entity_type} at position {i} follows {prev}')     return errors.

Count how many times each label appears across your dataset. Flag any entity type that appears in fewer than 1% of total labels -- it likely needs more training examples.

from collections import Counter def check_distribution(all_labels):     counts = Counter(all_labels)     total = sum(counts.values())     for label, count in counts.most_common():         pct = 100 count / total *        flag = ' ** RARE **' if pct < 1.0 and label != 'O' else ''         print(f'  {label}: {count} ({pct:.1f}%){flag}').

Coordinates should fall within the page dimensions, and no bounding box should have zero or negative width or height:.

def validate_bboxes(words, page_w=1000, page_h=1000):     complications = []     for w in words:         x0, y0, x1, y1 = w['bbox']         if x1 <= x0 or y1 <= y0:             issues.append(f"Zero/negative size: {w['text']}")         if x0 < 0 or y0 < 0 or x1 > page_w or y1 > page_h:             issues.append(f"Out of bounds: {w['text']}")     return issues.

This depends on your document diversity and label count, but here are practical benchmarks based on fine-tuning LayoutLMv3 from a pre-trained checkpoint:.

Single layout (e.g., one vendor's invoices).

Good accuracy on similar layouts.

Multi-type (invoices + receipts).

These numbers assume fine-tuning from a pre-trained checkpoint, not training from scratch. Starting with a checkpoint like LayoutLMv3-base gives you document layout understanding for free -- your BIO-tagged data just teaches it which fields to extract from your specific document types.

Recent findings suggest that start small. Label 50 documents, train a model, check the error patterns, fix your taxonomy if needed, then scale up. Labeling 1,000 documents with a flawed taxonomy wastes more time than labeling 50 documents twice.

According to recent reports, once your data is tagged and validated, the training pipeline is straightforward. Here's the outline using Hugging Face Transformers:.

from transformers import (     LayoutLMv3ForTokenClassification,     LayoutLMv3Processor,     TrainingArguments,     Trainer ) \.

model = LayoutLMv3ForTokenClassification.from_pretrained(     'microsoft/layoutlmv3-base',     num_labels=len(label_list)  # your BIO labels ) \.

args = TrainingArguments(     output_dir='./results',     num_train_epochs=30,     per_device_train_batch_size=4,     learning_rate=5e-5,     evaluation_strategy='epoch',     save_strategy='epoch',     load_best_model_at_end=True ) \.

trainer = Trainer(     model=model,     args=args,     train_dataset=train_data,     eval_dataset=val_data ) trainer.train().

The key hyperparameters to tune are learning rate (start with 5e-5), batch size (4 or 8 depending on GPU memory), and number of epochs (30 is a good starting point for small datasets). Use an 80/10/10 train/validation/test split, and make sure document types are distributed across all three splits.

It has been revealed that ● BIO tagging assigns B (beginning), I (inside), or O (outside) to every token. It's the standard labeling scheme for token classification in document AI.

● Pair BIO labels with normalized bounding box coordinates so models learn both textual and spatial patterns.

According to recent reports, ● Design your label taxonomy before you start annotating. One label per semantic meaning, hierarchical names, and a catch-all O label.

● Validate early. Check BIO sequence integrity, label distribution, and bounding box coordinates before training.

According to recent reports, ● Start with 50-100 labeled documents, train a model, check errors, and scale up. Quality matters more than quantity.

Sources indicate that ● Use pre-labeling (regex or model-based) to speed up annotation. Manual labeling from scratch doesn't scale.

The annotation step is the foundation of every document AI pipeline. The model you train is only as good as the BIO labels you feed it. Take the time to build a clean taxonomy, label consistently, and validate before training -- it saves debugging time later and produces models that actually work in production.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that utah has sued the companies behind the Stake sweepstakes site, alleging it ran an illegal casino for Utahns since 2022.
  • The timing of Utah’s suit against Stake stands out.
  • Utah Attorney General Derek Brown and the Utah Department of Commerce’s Division of Consumer Protection brought the case.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that utah has sued the companies behind the Stake sweepstakes site, alleging it ran an illegal casino for Utahns since 2022. The case follows Florida's own suit against Stake and adds to the legal pressure on the dual-currency sweepstakes model.

The timing of Utah’s suit against Stake stands out. Stake added Utah to its list of restricted states on Nov. 13, four days before the suit was filed, yet state consumer protection investigators could still use the site as recently as Nov. 16, when a banner noted access would end on Dec. 7, the 43-page complaint states.

Utah Attorney General Derek Brown and the Utah Department of Commerce’s Division of Consumer Protection brought the case. It names two defendants: Sweepsteaks Limited, based in Cyprus, and its Australian parent, Easygo Group Holdings Pty Ltd. The state refers to them jointly as Stake.

Sources indicate that the central allegation is that Stake has offered Utahns a round-the-clock casino since 2022. Utah has prohibited gambling since it became a state, and its Constitution bans gambling.

The complaint takes aim at how the site works. Players spend real money on two virtual currencies.

It has been revealed that utah wants the court to declare the site illegal gambling under state law. It also asks the court to bar Stake from offering its games in Utah and to order the company to return money taken from residents. The state is also seeking fines under the Utah Consumer Sales Practices Act and a remedy for harm to the public. The complaint adds claims for unjust enrichment, public nuisance and declaratory judgment.

It has been revealed that A demand that players’ losses be repaid raises the stakes for the wider industry. Taken together, the relief Utah seeks increases the legal risk for sweepstakes operators, suppliers and affiliates nationwide.

Utah is not the only state to bring Stake itself into court. Florida’s suit is broader in scope. It names Sweepsteaks Ltd and Easygo alongside Medium Rare and Kick Streaming, NEXT.io reported. It also names co-founders Bijan Tehrani and Ed Craven, plus payment firms Praxis and Breeze Labs Payments. Utah’s complaint is limited to the two corporate defendants.

Other states have targeted the same business model through a different operator. Kentucky and Arkansas have both sued VGW, which runs its own dual-currency sweepstakes sites.

Sources indicate that the Stake case is separate from Utah’s clash with federal regulators over prediction markets. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission has sued Utah to stop the state from using its own laws to shut down CFTC-registered contract markets. The Stake suit also came less than three weeks after Utah filed criminal charges against Kalshi’s founders. Those charges include felony counts of online gambling promotion.

Court records did not list a lawyer for either defendant, and the company did not answer a request for comment on the suit.

Tech Report: Connecticut online casinos set $65.7 million record in first month at 20% tax rate

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, connecticut's online casino revenue reached a fresh high in October 2026, the first month taxed at a higher rate.
  • In a recent development, connecticut’s two online casino operators, DraftKings and FanDuel, beat the previous record of $59.7 million, set in March, by about 10%.
  • It has been revealed that wagering grew as well.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, connecticut's online casino revenue reached a fresh high in October 2026, the first month taxed at a higher rate. Growth in the state sped up while the national market has been cooling.

In a recent development, connecticut’s two online casino operators, DraftKings and FanDuel, beat the previous record of $59.7 million, set in March, by about 10%. October revenue was also nearly $10 million higher than September’s total.

It has been revealed that wagering grew as well. Online casino handle topped $2 billion for the first time and was up 10% from October 2025. Revenue grew faster than handle in the month. That is consistent with operators keeping a larger share of each dollar wagered.

According to recent reports, the October result runs against a cooling national picture. US iGaming revenue grew 12% year over year in Q3 2026, the slowest rate on record, SiGMA World reported. Connecticut grew at that same 12% pace in the quarter.

Industry observers note that the American Gaming Association’s tracker reveals US iGaming revenue hit a record $3.05 billion in Q3 2026, up 13.5%. That was still the slowest quarterly growth since 2018. Connecticut had been part of the stronger phase. Its iGaming revenue reached $707.5 million in 2025, a 31.7% increase from 2024.

The jump from single-digit growth in September to a latest high a month later stands out. It suggests the national slowdown is not uniform across states. One month, however, does not set a trend.

Operators paid the state 18% of online casino gross gaming revenue through September 2026. They owe 20% for every period after that, the Department of Consumer Protection’s dataset notes show. That lower rate covered the five years after online casino gaming began on October 12, 2021.

In a recent development, the state’s take was already sizable before the increase. Online casino operators paid Connecticut $108,265,925 in 2025. Operators can still deduct some promotional credits before tax. That deduction has been capped at 15% of win since October 2023.

October’s figures show the higher rate did not coincide with any immediate drop in revenue. That matters for other states weighing online casino tax rates. It also matters for the two operators, which now share a larger tax bill in a market they split almost evenly.

Connecticut online casino wagers passed $2 billion in October, a record, in the first month taxed at 20% rather than 18%, according to state data. pic.twitter.com/FpO6DdEDUU.

— iGaming Times (@igaming_times) November 19, 2026.

October was only the second month in the past 12 in which DraftKings, rather than FanDuel, took the larger share of Connecticut online casino revenue, according to Poker Industry PRO. FanDuel has led the state in most months over that period.

It has been revealed that operators must send each month’s online casino payment to the state by the 15th of the following month. The first payment at the 20% rate was due by November 15, 2026. Payments on November revenue fall due by the 15th of December.
